For immunocompromised individuals, the recommended treatment for genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection includes the following options: acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 5 days, valacyclovir 500 mg orally twice daily for 5 days, or famciclovir 500 mg orally twice daily for 5 days. While the therapeutic benefits of these medications are likely similar, acyclovir is preferred due to its lower cost compared to valacyclovir and famciclovir. The choice of dosage may also depend on patient compliance considerations. This recommendation is conditional and based on moderate-quality evidence. 2. For adults and adolescents experiencing frequent, severe, or distressing recurrent clinical episodes of genital HSV infection, the World Health Organization (WHO) sexually transmitted infection (STI) guidelines recommend suppressive therapy over episodic therapy. Reassessment of the treatment approach is advised after one year. Patients experiencing four to six episodes per year or more, or those with severe symptoms causing significant distress, are more likely to benefit from suppressive therapy. Monitoring the frequency and severity of episodes during the initial months can help guide treatment decisions. This recommendation is conditional and supported by moderate-quality evidence. 3. For suppressive therapy in recurrent genital HSV infections, the WHO STI guidelines suggest acyclovir as the preferred medication over valacyclovir or famciclovir, primarily due to cost considerations. Although the therapeutic benefits of these drugs are comparable, acyclovir is more cost-effective. This recommendation is conditional and based on low-quality evidence. 4. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) represent a significant global public health challenge, adversely affecting quality of life and contributing to substantial morbidity and mortality. STIs directly impact reproductive and child health through complications such as infertility, cancers, and pregnancy-related issues. Indirectly, they facilitate the sexual transmission of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), thereby influencing both national and individual economic burdens. 5. Prevention and control of STIs are integral to comprehensive sexual and reproductive health services, which are essential for achieving universal health coverage as outlined in Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) No. 8. Globally, over one million curable STIs are acquired daily. In 2012, an estimated 357 million new cases of curable STIs occurred among adults aged 15–49 years, including 131 million cases of chlamydia, 78 million cases of gonorrhea, 6 million cases of syphilis, and 142 million cases of trichomoniasis. 6. The prevalence of viral STIs is also high, with approximately 417 million people infected with herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) and around 291 million women harboring human papillomavirus (HPV) at any given time. The burden of STIs varies by region and gender, with the highest impact observed in resource-poor countries. 7. If left undiagnosed and untreated, curable STIs can lead to severe complications, including pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, fetal loss, and congenital infections. In 2012, maternal syphilis infections were estimated to result in 350,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes, including stillbirths, neonatal deaths, preterm births, and infected infants. 8. Curable STIs accounted for nearly 11 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost in 2010. The psychological consequences of STIs include stigma, shame, and diminished self-worth. Certain STIs, such as syphilis and chancroid, significantly increase the risk of HIV acquisition, while non-ulcerative STIs like gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis enhance HIV transmission through genital shedding of the virus. 9. Effective treatment of STIs with appropriate medications at the right time is crucial for reducing HIV transmission and improving sexual and reproductive health. Strengthening STI diagnosis and treatment efforts is essential to achieve these goals. 10. Since the publication of the 2003 WHO guidelines for STI management, changes in STI epidemiology and advancements in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment necessitate updates to STI management protocols. Updated global guidance reflecting the latest evidence and expert opinion is required to assist countries in developing effective national approaches to STI prevention and treatment. 11. There is an urgent need to address the changing patterns of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in STIs, particularly for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. High-level resistance to quinolones, previously recommended as first-line treatment, is widespread, and decreased susceptibility to third-generation cephalosporins is increasing. Resistance to azithromycin has been reported in some strains of Treponema pallidum, and treatment failures have been observed with tetracyclines and macrolides in Chlamydia trachomatis infections. 12. The chronic and lifelong nature of viral infections like HSV-2 requires renewed attention to prevention strategies, including expanding access to available vaccines for HPV and developing new vaccines for HSV-2. Suppressive therapy for HSV-2 should be considered in areas with high HIV prevalence. 13. The syndromic approach to STI management, recommended in the 2003 WHO guidelines, involves diagnosing STIs based on consistent symptom groups and easily recognized signs, followed by treatment targeting the majority of causative organisms. However, these algorithms need updating to reflect the changing epidemiology of STIs. 14. Rapid point-of-care diagnostic tests (POCTs) are transforming STI management by enabling earlier diagnosis and treatment initiation. Updated guidelines should incorporate these rapid tests into syndromic management and provide algorithms for testing and screening. 15. Despite recent technological advances in diagnostics, therapeutics, vaccines, and barrier methods, access to these technologies remains limited, particularly in high-burden areas. Global STI management guidelines must address settings with limited access to modern technologies while also accommodating regions where these technologies are available. 16. Countries are strongly encouraged to adopt updated global guidance when establishing standardized national protocols, adapting these recommendations to local epidemiological and antimicrobial susceptibility data. Standardization ensures adequate treatment for all patients, optimizes healthcare provider training, and facilitates medicine procurement. 17. The WHO plans a phased approach to updating STI guidelines, addressing specific infections and issues in each phase. Phase 1 focuses on treatment recommendations for specific STIs, including chlamydia, gonorrhea, HSV-2, and syphilis, as well as syndromic management and clinical management packages. Subsequent phases will address STI prevention, additional infections, and laboratory diagnosis and screening.
